 With permanent daylight saving time, road safety imperative: Island Health
 Published 3:00 pm Thursday, November 19, 2026
 By Karl Yu 
 With increased darkness due to permanent daylight saving time, Island Health is preaching increased road safety. 
 (News Bulletin file photo) 
 Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... 
 With clocks in B.C. not rolled back an hour due to permanent Pacific Time, Island Health advises people to be mindful when driving, walking or cycling due to increased darkness.
 A majority of the Pacific timezone changed time on Nov. 1, but it didn’t apply to the province of B.C. due to a move by the government announced last March .
 In a press release, the health authority said people should exercise caution, slowing down, being alert, using vehicle lights and wearing clothing with reflectors, when moving via foot or motorized and non-motorized vehicles.
 “Pedestrian injuries and fatalities are more common during the fall and winter months in many places including in the Island Health region,” the press release noted. “Many factors may contribute to this seasonal pattern, including weather, changing travel habits and reduced visibility. Research shows that darkness and lower ambient light can make it more difficult for drivers to detect and react to people … at crossings and intersections.” 
 Drivers are advised to clean and defrost all windshields, windows and mirrors before travelling and slow down before intersections and where pedestrians are known to be walking. Assume that people will be harder to distinguish due to the dark and lower light and be extra vigilant at bus stops, school zones and crosswalks.
 If walking, jogging or running, Island Health asks that reflectors be worn on wrists, ankles and “where natural body movement puts [the] reflective devices into motion” increasing their visibility. Pedestrians are advised to be cautious, even if they have the right-of-way, as many pedestrians are struck “when they are legally crossing.” Further, making eye contact with drivers and not darting out if people are “running late and may miss [their] bus,” are also recommendations.
 In addition to the aforementioned reflective clothing, cyclists should utilize a white light at the front of their bicycles and a red light at the rear are advised, with lighting used at dawn, dusk and any situations where there is low lighting.
 There were close to 6,000 crashes on Vancouver Island that led to injury or death in 2025, stated the press release, and according to Dr. Melissa Wan, Island Health medical health officer, heeding the advice can prevent injuries and increase safety.
 “We can all take preventative actions to improve visibility, giving others more time to see one another and react safely,” Wan stated in the press release. “Whether you’re behind the wheel, on a bike, or on foot, slowing down, staying alert and making yourself visible can help create safer journeys for everyone.”
